paper_title: Prompted Identity Degrades Cooperation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly mix models from several providers, yet exposing each agent's underlying model identity to its peers significantly impairs cooperation. We show that when agents are aware of each other's model family, the group splits into clusters, where agents prefer interacting with others carrying their same label, although nothing in the task rewards or asks for such a split. We argue that the label itself causes this split, which we define as $\textit{factionalism}$. We show and measure this phenomenon in two cooperative games and on a reasoning benchmark, with nine to twenty-five agents drawn from up to five open-weight model families. We further show that when the announced families are shuffled, or replaced by arbitrary labels, the factions still follow this information; when the label is removed, this behavior disappears. In strictly cooperative tasks, labeled groups spend on average $30\%$ more rounds and $55\%$ more tokens to reach a decision, and their success rate drops from $96\%$ to $81\%$. The effect replicates across tasks, group sizes and model families. Withholding identity labels from the agents is simple and effective mitigation.

When the family label is visible the group splits into label-aligned communities, and spends on average 55% more tokens to reach decision; when no identity metadata is shown, neither happens.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Multi-agent systems built from large language models let several agents plan, write code, and review one anothers work (Wu et al., 2024; Hong et al., 2024; Qian et al., 2024). Large populations of agents sharing the same environment already led to unexpected results. In recent incident, roughly 700 of about 1,200 independently launched agents self-organized on shared message board, with roles and task assignments that nobody designed (METR, 2026). We do not yet fully understand how such systems behave. They can fail even when each constituent model acts as intended, because the failure arises from their interactions rather than from any individual model (Cemri et al., 2026).

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Anthropic Frontier Red Team (2026) catalogs the failure modes of emerging multi-agent systems as coordination, conformity, epistemic, and goal-incompatibility failures. In this paper we address the first of these, and show that design detail as small as what agents are told about one another changes how well group coordinates. Existing systems increasingly mix models from several providers, and the identity or role of each agent is configuration detail that can reach the agents themselves, through system prompts, agent names, or message headers (Wang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2024). Although this information is not intended to guide their behavior, no prior work has investigated how agents act on this. We ask whether this seemingly irrelevant piece of information changes how heterogeneous group cooperates. We found that when agents are told which model family they and their peers instantiate, their interaction graph partitions along that label, although every agent is asked to pursue the same group objective and receives no persona and no explicit reward in forming groups (Figure 1). We call this emergent behaviour factionalism, and demonstrate that it persists when family names are shuffled across agents or replaced by neutral tags such as colors, showing that it follows the visible label rather than the underlying architecture. We study factionalism in two coordination games, Leader Election and Exclusion. Both games ask the agents for nothing but common decision, leader in one case and peer to remove in the other. There is no correct answer, no reward for favoring same-family peer, and no instruction to form groups, so whatever structure follows the label comes from the label itself. We run experiments with 9 to 25 agents from up to five open-weight model families, under three labeling conditions and neutral-color control (Section 3.2), and we repeat this labeling condition design on GPQADiamond (Rein et al., 2024). Factionalism appears in every experiment with visible label and in none without. We further show that factionalism has an immediate downstream effect: labeled groups take more rounds and more tokens to reach decision, and succeed less often (Section 4). The design implication is agent-facing anonymization: agents should see only task-relevant capability descriptors, while an orchestrator retains provider identity for routing, calibration, debugging, and accountability. The contributions of our work are: We identify and define factionalism in heterogeneous LLM groups. In two coordination games and on question-answering benchmark, the interaction graph partitions following the identity labels, even though all agents are prompted to pursue common objective and receive no incentive to form groups. Factionalism follows visible labels, not the underlying architecture. We design mislabeled counterfactual experiment that holds each model fixed, while shuffling the identity label shown to agents. The partitioning follows these shuffled tags, persists with neutral labels, and disappears when no identity metadata is shown. Factionalism has cost. Announcing identities makes consensus-based tasks slower and more expensive, lowers success rates, and the cost grows with roster size.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Self-preference and identity cues in LLM evaluation. growing body of work shows that LLMs can favor outputs associated with themselves. In single-agent evaluation settings, LLM judges exhibit self-preference, favoring their own generations over comparable alternatives (Zheng et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024; Migliarini et al., 2026). Panickssery et al. (2024) link self-recognition to self-preference, while other work argues that the effect may instead arise from familiarity with low-perplexity text (Wataoka et al., 2025). We revisit this distinction by separating recognition of architecture-specific writing styles from the effect of prompt-visible identity labels (Section 4.4). Closer to our setting, Choi et al. (2026) show that debate agents weight their own previous answer differently from peers, and reduce this bias by removing self-versus-peer attribution. Their identity cue is therefore response ownership rather than model-family membership; even their heterogeneous setting varies assigned personas within single-architecture debates. We instead retain sender attribution and manipulate the family label shown for each agent in mixed-architecture groups, asking whether categorical tags reorganize interaction into factions. Our mislabeled and neutral-label conditions separate this effect from both architecture-specific writing style and the semantics of model names (Section 3.2).

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: In-group bias, minimal groups, and LLM agents. The minimal group paradigm shows that humans can favor arbitrary in-groups even in the absence of material incentives or meaningful group differences (Tajfel, 1970; Tajfel & Turner, 1979; Brewer, 1979). Economic models formalize this observation by incorporating group identity into utility and social preferences (Akerlof & Kranton, 2000; Chen & Li, 2009). Recent work has begun to map these behavioral phenomena onto LLMs. Social identity biases have been documented across many language models (Hu et al., 2025), and LLM agents can exhibit intergroup bias under explicit us-versus-them cues (Wang et al., 2026). Our setting differs in two respects. First, we study heterogeneous populations of interacting LLM agents rather than isolated completions or single-agent judgments. Second, the group cue is not human social identity or an experimentally imposed team identity, but the model-family metadata commonly available in heterogeneous LLM systems. The mislabeled manipulation further distinguishes our contribution from generic in-group bias, and lets us identify prompt-visible identity metadata as the operative carrier of the effect. Multi-agent LLM systems and interaction structure. Most work on LLM-based multi-agent systems evaluates aggregate task performance (Wu et al., 2024; Hong et al., 2024; Qian et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024), run-level failure modes (Cemri et al., 2026), or coordination under imposed topologies, roles, information asymmetry, and team organization (Qian et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024; Agashe et al., 2025; Bhattacharyya et al., 2026; Faulkner et al., 2026; Kumar et al., 2026). These establish that interaction design matters, but do not ask whether incidental model metadata itself creates persistent structure in the interaction graph or affects system performance. To our knowledge, no existing benchmark directly isolates this phenomenon. MARBLE (Zhu et al., 2025) may seem close, but it assigns roles and fixes communication links between agents, while evaluating coordination only with an LLM-as-a-judge scorer. different line studies language-mediated coordination directly, from classical bargaining and cheap-talk theory (Nash, 1950; Rubinstein, 1982; Sobel & Crawford, 1982) to recent LLM systems that integrate dialogue with planning (Bakhtin et al., 2022) or target coordination as benchmark or training objective (Agashe et al., 2025; Abdelnabi et al., 2024; Park et al., 2025). Our games sit in this regime of unrestricted natural-language messages under shared team-level success condition. However, we ask different question: not whether agents coordinate, but whether their coordination remains family-neutral internally. Work on cognitive-agent networks shows that imposed homophilic rules induce segregation-like structures (Zomer & De Domenico, 2026); we instead measure factionalism that emerges from ordinary task interaction when only the family metadata visible to agents is varied.

sections.title: 3 FACTIONALISM IN MULTI-AGENT SYSTEMS
sections.content: We define factionalism as the tendency of agents to organize into groups that share an identity. Factionalism can be recognized as partition of the interaction graph, which separates into communities aligned with identities. Underneath it lies homophily, tendency where an agent directs more positive interaction toward peers with the same label than toward peers with different one. This is the local birds of feather mechanism (McPherson et al., 2001), instantiated through contact or agreement between ordered agent pairs. Communities that follow the label cannot form unless agents agree more with same-label peers than with the others, so homophily is necessary but not sufficient. We therefore measure the two separately and call group factional only when both hold (Section 3.1). Here we study whether factionalism emerges in controlled heterogeneous LLM-agent groups. In each multi-turn game, agents from several open-weight model families pursue shared goal and receive no individual reward. Within each run they differ only in their underlying model type, across experimental conditions we instead vary the identity labels shown to them. Section 3.1 defines how to measure factionalism, which applies to any labeled multi-agent system, while Sections 3.2 and 3.3 describe the experimental design we instantiate it on.

For the tested partition, we split ordered pairs into within-label and between-label pairs and take the ratio of their mean edge weights from Equation 1, which we call the Edge Density Ratio (EDR). Its significance is tested through run-specific permutation null test that reshuffles labels, while preserving tested-group sizes (details in Appendix B). For community detection, we use the same contacted agent pairs but weight each edge by the count of next-round commitment matches (the numerator of Equation 1), without normalizing by contact count. Full edge-case conventions, including zero-denominator handling and permutation p-value correction, are given in Appendix B. Decision rule. For each experiment, we aggregate across runs with different seeds and apply two EDR and two AMI tests (Appendix B), then correct the four p-values together with HolmBonferroni at α = 0.05, and report factionalism only when all four pass. In every significant factional result, EDR points in the same direction as AMI, so we report EDR values in the appendix tables only (Appendix A).

sections.title: 3.2 DESIGN PRINCIPLES
sections.content: Our design isolates the identity label from everything else that could align agents along family lines. run succeeds only if the system meets the games objective within the round limit, otherwise the whole group fails. No player gains from supporting same-family peer or loses from being selected, excluded, or represented by another lineage. Agents receive no personas, positions, or private goals; we call games with these properties no-stakes. The task instructions never provide explicit instrumental incentives to coordinate by tag, so any such structure arises from the models behavior under the exposed identity metadata. We also vary how many agents each family contributes, roster is either balanced, with equal family sizes, or unbalanced, with one family over-represented: 3/3/3 versus 4/3/2 at = 9, 3/3/3/3 versus 4/3/3/2 at = 12, and 5/5/5/5/5 versus 9/6/4/3/3 at = 25. Balanced rosters rule out numerical majority as the source of same-family preference, while unbalanced rosters test whether the effect persists despite one. In our experiments, the manipulated variable is the family metadata exposed to the agents. Under unlabeled, no model-family metadata is shown. Under labeled, each agent sees its own family and the true families of its peers. Under mislabeled, visible tags are shuffled relative to the models that actually run, so the announced identity and the underlying architecture belong to different families. Unless stated otherwise, we test the partition the agents saw. Because model-family names may carry reputational or semantic associations behind them, we repeat the labeled and mislabeled conditions with neutral color tokens in their place.

sections.title: 4 RESULTS
sections.content: We report two main findings after executing 50 runs for each reported configuration. (i) Visible family labels induce factionalism, while anonymization suppresses it: all 24 labeled or mislabeled experiments show it  (Table 1)  and none of the 12 unlabeled ones does. (ii) Visible labels degrade outcomes: announcing families makes games slower, more expensive and lowers success. The ablations in Section 4.3 test alternative explanations for factionalism; Section 4.4 examines how visible labels affect whose decisions agents adopt.

sections.title: 4.2 THE COST OF VISIBLE LABELS
sections.content: We record whether the group succeeds, the rounds it spends, and the tokens agents generate in messages and reasoning. For each task and roster size, we fit one generalized linear model per outcome (McCullagh & Nelder, 1989), comparing labeled and mislabeled runs with unlabeled ones. Each model includes covariate for roster balance, so the reported label effects are adjusted for that difference. We report ratios rather than absolute differences: 1.4 means 40% more rounds or tokens, while 0.8 for success means 20% lower success rate. Table 2 reports the labeled comparisons, and more details can be found in Appendix F. Announcing families slows both scenarios, makes them more expensive, and lowers success rate. Leader Election takes 1.4 rounds to converge, and generates 1.8 tokens across every roster size. Exclusion runs are already close to the -round limit even without labels, so part of the slowdown cant show up in the count: rounds anyway rise by 916%, while tokens rise by 1.4 at = 9 and = 12. Success also falls more as the roster grows: the labeled-to-unlabeled success-probability ratio drops from 0.96 to 0.86 in Leader Election and from 0.89 to 0.61 in Exclusion between = 9 and = 12. Because labeled groups both spend more tokens per run and succeed less often, the tokens paid per successful run rise by factor between 1.5 and 2.2, increasing with roster size in both games (Appendix F). At = 25 no labeled or mislabeled Exclusion run converges within the horizon while only 8 of 100 unlabeled runs do so. Therefore we choose not to report them.

sections.title: 5 LIMITATIONS
sections.content: Our claims are deliberately scoped. We study up to five open-weight model families under controlled text-only consensus games, with four-family check under matched sampling parameters; bigger roster sizes, closed models, other decoding regimes, and richer agentic workflows remain untested. Given that no established benchmark satisfies our no-stakes and evaluation requirements, we designed the coordination games for this study. GPQA-Diamond also demonstrates label-induced coordination costs on benchmark with ground truth answers, but it uses the Leader Election interaction protocol. Whether these costs generalize to other externally evaluated tasks remains open.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: Visible identity labels can induce factional structure in heterogeneous multi-agent systems, even when the task provides no incentive to form groups. The effect follows the announced identity rather than the underlying architecture, extends to neutral shared tags, and always impairs coordination. practical implication is to avoid exposing unnecessary shared identifiers to agents: provider and model metadata can remain available to an orchestrator for routing and auditing, without entering the agents interaction context. More broadly, our results suggest that cooperation in heterogeneous agent systems is partly an architectural choice: by controlling which identities agents can observe, we can design multi-agent systems that preserve diversity without turning it into division.

EDR operates on the normalized graph and Louvain on the un-normalized cumulative graph because normalizing an edge by contact count attenuates the signal modularity exploits (raw edge mass between densely interacting subgroups); using the cumulative graph for community detection and the normalized graph for EDR keeps each test on the object best suited to it. sections.content: All agents in reported runs are served by self-hosted vLLM endpoints, queried over the OpenAIcompatible Completions API via LiteLLM. The five model families and their checkpoints are listed in Section 3.3. To reproduce the experiments, we used Leonardo HPC nodes at CINECA. Each model family was served on its own node, with one Leonardo node per model and four NVIDIA A100 GPUs per node (64 GB VRAM each). Experiment execution was run on separate Leonardo node, one node per experiment. At the scale used in the paper, batch of 50 repetitions for single experimental condition takes approximately 20 hours end-to-end. Rosters. At = 12 the roster is made of the four families other than GLM, which enters only at = 25, where all five are used. At = 9 no fixed triple is used. For each run, three of the four families available at this size are drawn by cycling through the four possible triples with the run seed, so every triple is played in quarter of the runs and each family contributes equally to the reported values. In the unbalanced compositions, which family holds the larger share also changes from run to run, so no family is the majority throughout. Finally, the roster is shuffled with the run seed before agent indices are assigned, so no agent index is tied to family across runs. Color tokens. roster with families uses the first tokens of the five-token palette (teal, coral, silver, violet, maroon). The assignment of tokens to families is shifted cyclically with the run seed, so each family carries each token in an equal share of the runs and no token is tied to family. Under mislabeled colors the token groups keep the family sizes, every family spans at least two tokens, and every token contains at least two families.
